marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q001.takeaway: The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous phase-4 depolarization and intrinsic firing rate.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q001.displayText:
The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous phase-4 depolarization and intrinsic firing rate.

The SA node acts as the pacemaker of the heart as it generates impulses at the highest rate (60-100/min), compared to AV node (40-60/min) and Purkinje fibres (15-40). The impulses generated by SA node are conducted through AV node and purkinje fibres repetedly that it will prevent AV node or Purkinje fibres reach their own thresholds for self-excitation.
emphasis: The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous phase-4 depolarization and intrinsic firing rate

rationales.a: Several cardiac pacemaker cells fire spontaneously, so automaticity alone does not explain SA dominance.
rationales.b: Sympathetic innervation modulates rate but does not establish the hierarchy.
rationales.d: The SA node is strongly vagally innervated; poor cholinergic innervation is not the reason.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q002.takeaway: AV nodal tissue conducts most slowly, creating the delay that allows ventricular filling before contraction.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q002.displayText:
AV nodal tissue conducts most slowly, creating the delay that allows ventricular filling before contraction.

The conduction velocity is least in AV node.
The slow conduction in the AV node is caused mainly by diminished numbers of gap junctions between successive cells in the conducting pathways.
emphasis: AV nodal tissue conducts most slowly, creating the delay that allows ventricular filling before contraction

rationales.b: Ventricular myocardium conducts faster than AV nodal tissue.
rationales.c: The His bundle conducts more rapidly than the AV node.
rationales.d: Purkinje fibers have the fastest conduction velocity.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q003.takeaway: Purkinje fibers conduct impulses fastest to synchronize ventricular activation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q003.displayText:
Purkinje fibers conduct impulses fastest to synchronize ventricular activation.

The velocity of conduction of impulse is maximum in Purkinje fibers.
Purkinje fibers have the maximum number of gap junctions hence the maximum conduction velocity (4m/s).
emphasis: Purkinje fibers conduct impulses fastest to synchronize ventricular activation

rationales.a: Atrial muscle conduction is slower than specialized Purkinje conduction.
rationales.b: SA-node tissue conducts slowly relative to the His–Purkinje network.
rationales.c: AV nodal conduction is the slowest region, not the fastest.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q004.takeaway: AV nodal delay is approximately 0.1 second.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q004.displayText:
AV nodal delay is approximately 0.1 second.

The AV nodal delay is 0.1 second.
The slow conduction is caused mainly by diminished numbers of gap junctions between successive cells in the conducting pathways. It ensures that the atria have ejected their blood into the ventricles first before the ventricles contract.

rationales.a: 0.2 s is about twice the usual AV nodal delay.
rationales.c: 0.5 s would produce marked conduction block, not normal delay.
rationales.d: 0.01 s is too short to provide physiologic AV delay.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q005.takeaway: Normal ventricular activation reaches the LV basal epicardium about 0.22 s after SA-node discharge.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q005.displayText:
Normal ventricular activation reaches the LV basal epicardium about 0.22 s after SA-node discharge.

The duration of action potential to arrive at the epicardial surface at the base of the left ventricle is 0.22 sec.
Impulse initiated from SA node at 0.00 s.
Impulse reaches AV node at 0.03 s.
Delay of impulse at AV node by 0.13 s resulting in a total time of 0.16 s (0.03+0.13) to reach the beginning of Purkinje fibres.
Impulse reaches base of Purkinje fibres by 0.03 s resulting in a total time of 0.19 s (0.16+0.03) to reach the endocardial surface of the base of the ventricle.
Impulse travels from endocardial to epicardial surface in 0.03 s (due to arrangement of myocardial fibres).
Hence, a total time of 0.22 s (0.19+0.03) is taken for the impulse to travel from SA node to epicardial surface of the base of ventricles.
emphasis: Normal ventricular activation reaches the LV basal epicardium about 0

rationales.a: 0.16 s is earlier than the expected propagation time to the specified epicardial site.
rationales.b: 0.18 s is still earlier than the stated normal arrival.
rationales.d: 0.12 s is too early for atrial, nodal and ventricular conduction to complete.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q006.takeaway: Purkinje activation depolarizes septum first, then spreads from endocardium toward epicardium.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q006.displayText:
Purkinje activation depolarizes septum first, then spreads from endocardium toward epicardium.

The order of depolarization is from septum → endocardium → epicardium.
The spread of Cardiac Excitation:
Atrial depolarization is initiated from SA node, spreads radially through atria, then converges on the AV node. A delay of about 0.1 s (AV nodal delay) occurs before excitation spreads to the ventricles.
Ventricular depolarization starts at the left side of the interventricular septum and moves first to the right across the midportion of the septum. It moves along the ventricular walls to the AV groove, proceeding from the endocardial to the epicardial surface.
emphasis: Purkinje activation depolarizes septum first, then spreads from endocardium toward epicardium

rationales.b: The sequence does not start in endocardium before septal activation.
rationales.c: Epicardium is activated after the endocardial wave, not first.
rationales.d: Epicardial activation precedes endocardial activation in this option, reversing normal spread.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q007.takeaway: Phase 0 of a ventricular myocyte action potential is the fast Na⁺-dependent upstroke.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q007.displayText:
Phase 0 of a ventricular myocyte action potential is the fast Na⁺-dependent upstroke.

The action potential is most dependant on sodium permeability in phase 0.
Action potential of myocardium:
• Phase 0: Depolarisation: Influx of Na+ into myocyte.
• Phase 1: Early repolarization: Efflux of K+ from myocyte.
• Phase 2: Plateau: Ca2+ enters myocardial cells via voltage regulated L-type Ca2+ channels.
• Phase 3: Repolarisation: Efflux of K+.
• Phase 4: Restoration of RMP: Restoration of Na+ and K+ by Na-K ATPase.
emphasis: Phase 0 of a ventricular myocyte action potential is the fast Na⁺-dependent upstroke

rationales.a: Phase 3 repolarization is dominated by outward K⁺ currents.
rationales.b: Phase 2 plateau reflects Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux.
rationales.d: Phase 1 is early repolarization, not the fast sodium upstroke.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q008.takeaway: L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening sustains the ventricular action-potential plateau.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q008.displayText:
L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening sustains the ventricular action-potential plateau.

Plateau phase of ventricular muscle is due to opening of Ca channel.
Action potential of myocardium:
• Phase 0: Depolarisation: Influx of Na+ into myocyte.
• Phase 1: Early repolarization: Efflux of K+ from myocyte.
• Phase 2: Plateau: Ca2+ enters myocardial cells via voltage regulated L-type Ca2+ channels.
• Phase 3: Repolarisation: Efflux of K+.
• Phase 4: Restoration of RMP: Restoration of Na+ and K+ by Na-K ATPase.
emphasis: L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening sustains the ventricular action-potential plateau

rationales.a: Fast Na⁺ channels initiate phase 0, not the prolonged plateau.
rationales.c: K⁺ currents contribute to repolarization and balance the plateau Ca²⁺ current.
rationales.d: Cl⁻ channels do not generate the ventricular plateau.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q009.takeaway: Ventricular repolarization proceeds from epicardium toward endocardium because epicardial action potentials are shorter.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q009.displayText:
Ventricular repolarization proceeds from epicardium toward endocardium because epicardial action potentials are shorter.

Repolarization of cardiac muscle proceeds from epicardium to endocardium.
Depolarisation proceeds from endocardium to epicardium in an intact cardiac muscle.
emphasis: Ventricular repolarization proceeds from epicardium toward endocardium because epicardial action potentials are shorter

rationales.a: Repolarization is not a simple left-to-right wave.
rationales.b: Endocardium-to-epicardium describes depolarization direction, not repolarization.
rationales.d: The base-to-apex description is not the principal transmural repolarization direction.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q010.takeaway: Pacemaker-cell phase 0 is generated mainly by opening of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q010.displayText:
Pacemaker-cell phase 0 is generated mainly by opening of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.

Phase 0 of pacemaker potential is initiated by opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
The pacemaker potential consists of:
• Phase 0 - This is upstroke seen due to the opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. This causes an influx of calcium leading to the upstroke.
• Phase 3 - This is followed by inactivation of the calcium channels and simultaneous activation of K+ channels. This leads to efflux of K+ bringing about repolarization.
• Phase 4 - As the K+ efflux declines, a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+ opens leading to an influx of both Na+ and K+. This is the If channel. This is responsible for slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization. This accounts for the automaticity of SA and AV node.
The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.
Note: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels seen in myocyte potential are permanently inactivated because of the less negative resting potential of the pacemaker cells.
emphasis: Pacemaker-cell phase 0 is generated mainly by opening of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels

rationales.a: Fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels drive phase 0 in working myocytes, not nodal pacemaker cells.
rationales.c: Ca²⁺-channel inactivation contributes to repolarization, not the pacemaker upstroke.
rationales.d: Na⁺-channel inactivation is not the phase-0 mechanism in SA/AV pacemaker cells.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q011.takeaway: Vagal stimulation slows heart rate, increasing the R–R interval between successive ECG complexes.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q011.displayText:
Vagal stimulation slows heart rate, increasing the R–R interval between successive ECG complexes.

Vagal stimulation can cause an increase in the R-R interval in the ECG as it decreases heart rate.
emphasis: Vagal stimulation slows heart rate, increasing the R–R interval between successive ECG complexes

rationales.a: Vagal tone lowers heart rate rather than raising it.
rationales.c: Reduced heart rate usually lowers cardiac output if other variables are unchanged.
rationales.d: Vagal stimulation has little direct effect on ventricular contractility compared with sympathetic input.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q012.takeaway: Lead I records voltage between right arm negative and left arm positive electrodes.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q012.displayText:
Lead I records voltage between right arm negative and left arm positive electrodes.

In recording Lead I, the right arm is negative electrode and the positive electrode is left arm.
Bipolar Limb leads for ECG recording:
• LA → left arm
• RA → right arm
• LL → left foot
emphasis: Lead I records voltage between right arm negative and left arm positive electrodes

rationales.b: The left leg is the positive electrode for lead II, not lead I.
rationales.c: Right leg is the ground/reference electrode.
rationales.d: Lead I uses one positive left-arm electrode, not a combined limb average.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q013.takeaway: Einthoven’s law states lead II = lead I + lead III.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q013.displayText:
Einthoven’s law states lead II = lead I + lead III.

Einthoven's law states Lead I + Lead III = Lead II.
Einthoven's triangle is an imaginary formation of three limb leads in a triangle used in electrocardiography.
emphasis: Einthoven’s law states lead II = lead I + lead III

rationales.b: Lead I is lead II minus lead III, not their sum.
rationales.c: Lead III is lead II minus lead I.
rationales.d: Only the relation II=I+III is the direct law as written.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q014.takeaway: Lead III = lead II − lead I = 2−1 = 1 mV.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q014.displayText:
Lead III = lead II − lead I = 2−1 = 1 mV.

According to Einthoven's law,
Lead I + Lead III = Lead II.
Lead III = Lead II − Lead I = (2−1) = 1 mV.
emphasis: Lead III = lead II − lead I = 2−1 = 1 mV

rationales.b: 2 mV is the given lead II value, not lead III.
rationales.c: 3 mV adds leads I and II instead of applying Einthoven’s relation.
rationales.d: 4 mV has no basis in the lead relation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q015.takeaway: An augmented unipolar limb lead compares one explored limb with the average of the other two limbs.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q015.displayText:
An augmented unipolar limb lead compares one explored limb with the average of the other two limbs.

In a standard ECG, an augmented lead measures the electrical potential difference between one limb and the other two limbs. aVR, aVL, aVF are the augmented limb leads.
emphasis: An augmented unipolar limb lead compares one explored limb with the average of the other two limbs

rationales.a: A standard bipolar limb lead measures between two limbs; augmented leads use one vs the other two.
rationales.c: The reference is not a single neutral electrode.
rationales.d: The lead is one limb against a combined reference, not two limbs against two.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q016.takeaway: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q016.displayText:
The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.

The part of the ECG that corresponds to ventricular repolarization is T wave.
emphasis: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization

rationales.d: U wave, when present, follows T and may reflect late repolarization, not the main ventricular repolarization wave.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q017.takeaway: The PR interval spans atrial depolarization through AV nodal/His conduction to the start of ventricular depolarization.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q017.displayText:
The PR interval spans atrial depolarization through AV nodal/His conduction to the start of ventricular depolarization.

The PR interval indicates atrial depolarisation (P wave) and AV node conduction time (PR segment).
PR interval is the time between the beginning of the P wave and the beginning of the QRS complex. It is the interval between the beginning of electrical excitation of the atria and the beginning of excitation of the ventricles. Normal duration is 0.12-0.20 s.
emphasis: The PR interval spans atrial depolarization through AV nodal/His conduction to the start of ventricular depolarization

rationales.a: Atrial depolarization is included, but alone does not define the full PR interval.
rationales.b: Ventricular repolarization is represented by T wave, not PR interval.
rationales.c: AV nodal conduction contributes, but atrial activation is also included.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q018.takeaway: Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves because atrial activation is chaotic.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q018.displayText:
Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves because atrial activation is chaotic.

The P wave is absent in atrial fibrillation.
In atrial fibrillation, numerous small depolarization waves spread in all directions through the atria. The waves are weak and many of them are of opposite polarity at any given time, they almost electrically neutralize one another. Therefore, P waves are absent from ECG in atrial fibrillation.
emphasis: Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves because atrial activation is chaotic

rationales.b: Atrial flutter usually has organized sawtooth flutter waves rather than absent atrial activity.
rationales.c: Congestive failure alone does not abolish P waves.
rationales.d: WPW changes ventricular activation and PR/QRS patterns but P waves remain.
